idiom_name: sealed interface node hierarchy with val properties + exhaustive when
implementation_notes: Kotlin's sealed hierarchies give the node set to the compiler: sealed interface Expr with data class Binary(val left: Expr, val op: String, val right: Expr) declares the named, typed children directly, and when (node) over them is checked exhaustively with no else branch (the compiler's own PSI uses the same interface-plus-named-accessor shape). This replaces both the instanceof chains and the visitor scaffolding of the classic structure; keep a classic visitor only when third parties must add operations without touching the nodes.
code_sketch:
sealed interface Expr
data class Literal(val value: Int) : Expr
data class Binary(val left: Expr, val op: String, val right: Expr) : Expr   // named children

fun print(e: Expr): String = when (e) {                     // exhaustive, no else
    is Literal -> e.value.toString()
    is Binary  -> "(${print(e.left)} ${e.op} ${print(e.right)})"
}
pitfalls: Data classes generate structural equality and hashCode that recurse through children: comparing two large trees is surprisingly expensive and can overflow the stack.
A when used as a statement, or one that mixes a non-sealed branch in, loses exhaustiveness and silently grows an else path.
Sealed subclasses must live in the same package and module, so users of the library cannot extend the node set.
